extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical literature; those studying Roman poetry, prose, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for assessing Roman poetry, drama, epic subject-choice, and prose style, drawn from a lecture-format literary history of Rome. Emphasizes originality, national character, suitability of form, and stylistic virtues in different genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid close imitation of individual models
rubrics_metrics.description: The close imitation of any individual model never failed to produce disagreeable consequences: and of this we have a striking example in Sallust, whose strict imitation of Thucydides has gone far to lessen the effect of his own great original genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strictly copying another author's manner or model reduces originality and the effect of an author's native genius; imitation can produce 'forced' style and elaborate artifice. Authors should be wary of transplanting a single foreign model wholesale into their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, consistency, and delicacy of propriety in historical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: In the drawing of characters, and indeed, in general, as a historical painter, Sallust has few equals; but he is neither so clear nor so consistent a writer, nor endued with so delicate a sense of propriety, as Caesar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical prose should aim for clear expression, internal consistency, and a refined sense of propriety; these qualities are central to judging the success of historical narration and character-drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature should reflect national character and appropriate subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: To dwell on rural enjoyments, and make use of simple feelings, therefore, was quite necessary for one who aspired to be the poet not of the metropolis, but of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national poet should treat subjects and modes of life that resonate with the nation's character (e.g., rural/agricultural life for Rome) so as to secure broad and lasting national sympathy and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama must assume a character conformable to national manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage which aspires to exert an universal influence, must assume a character conformable to the manners, education, temper, and modes of thinking, which prevail among the nation who are to survey its exhibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not simply imitate foreign dramatic forms; adapt dramatic style and content to the manners, education, and temper of the local audience. The power of drama is proportional to how peculiar and fitting it is to its nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical poetry must be the free emanation of individual feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole charm and excellence of this sort of writing consists, in its being the free emanation of individual feelings. The whole beauty of it vanishes the moment we detect a single trace of imitation; it is only tolerable because it is natural, and the appearance of art renders it immediately disgusting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyrical poets must prioritize naturalness and personal feeling over artful imitation; detectable borrowing of lines or mannerisms from models destroys the lyric's charm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic subject selection: prefer events that allow feeling and audacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical event which is to form the subject of an epic poem should be one wherein feeling and audacity seem to have exerted a more predominant influence than reasoning and calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose epic subjects that permit grand imagination and bold action (e.g., Alexander, the fall of Darius); avoid subjects that are mainly political contests of parties where heroic unity and imaginative play are lacking (e.g., Roman civil wars). The nature of the incidents matters more than their chronological proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and harmonious arrangement of parts in epic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If he had only given to agriculture and rural feelings as prominent a place in his great work... the heroic traditions... would have then obtained a faster hold on our feelings, and a closer connection with the thoughts of all men and all ages... In the very stiff arrangement which he has adopted, the latter part of his poem ... appears to infinite disadvantage when compared with the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic structure should achieve organic unity and natural connection between parts; stiff or artificial arrangements dissipate the work's spirit and produce imbalance between sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that rigid imitation of Homer or other models can weaken epic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid imitation of Homer has weakened and confined the genius of Virgil, and drawn both him and many more recent poets into the most glaring errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While classical models can inform technique, slavish replication of an exemplar's form and manner limits a poet's originality and may introduce glaring faults; adapt rather than copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire and depiction of common life: drama preferred for full picture
rubrics_metrics.description: The only perfect picture which poetry can set before us of common life, is in the drama: individual traits or scenes, however masterly, can never satisfy us. The Roman satire, therefore, in the hands of such a writer as Horace, is merely a substitute for that comedy which the Roman people ought to have possessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comprehensive depictions of common life, drama is the most effective form; satire functions as a partial substitute by focusing on urban manners and corruption. When using satire, center on social habits, spectacles, and the corruption of manners typical of urban life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match prose stylistic qualities to authorial aims (language purity and suitability)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Caesar it appears in unadorned simplicity and greatness; in Livy it wears all the splendour and ornament of elaborate rhetoric, but is still free from exaggeration, beautiful and noble in its construction; in Tacitus ... it assumes an appearance of depth, power, and energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prose according to appropriate virtues for its kind: simplicity and grandeur for concise political narrative (Caesar), polished rhetorical splendour for elaborate history (Livy), and concentrated depth and energy for penetrating analysis (Tacitus). Style should serve substance.
